results.question: What do the screen-combat and fight-choreography books say about making a punch read as re
results.answer:
The books treat punch realism as one physics illusion with three coordinated parts: camera geometry hides the fact that no contact happens, the victim's reaction creates the impact, and timing binds attack and reaction so they read as a single cause-and-effect event.

## Angle and distance: hiding the miss

The core trick is choosing between two geometries. In an over-the-shoulder shot, the attacker punches almost at the target but aims a tiny bit toward the camera, staying out of distance so they can't physically land it; in a profile two-shot, they're genuinely in range but punch offline, past the face — the classic "**parrot punch**," aimed at the imaginary parrot on the victim's shoulder [S4]. The illusion holds because the fist-to-face relationship relative to the camera stays identical as the angle changes; only the performer's felt geometry shifts between "out of distance, on target" and "in distance, off target," with diagonals blending the two [S4]. On a straight profile either side of the head works, but once you go diagonal you must commit to the side nearer the camera — the far side sits too far from the lens line to sell [S4].

Angle and distance remain artistic choices, but the frame still has to deliver the information the illusion needs [S2]. Non-contact hits are unforgiving on this front: any contradiction between the attack's angle or force and the reaction reads instantly, mistakes in timing make hits look like misses, and these techniques sell poorly in close-up, slow motion, or 3D [S8]. Wide, sweeping, circular action also photographs better than short, straight techniques, even when the straight version is more powerful in reality [S11], and since every change in angle or framing forces a choreography adjustment, cuts need a genuine shift in camera placement to avoid jarring [S13].

## The reaction: the victim sells the hit

The person taking the punch does most of the work. With real contact they get tactile cues for when and where; with non-contact hits they have no information at all and must sell the entire effect through acting, which demands far more skill from the receiver [S8]. Good choreography then separates the physics from the choice: an involuntary recoil — torso jerk, impulse proxy — followed by a deliberate "**decision beat**" before the body surrenders and falls [S5]. The camera can join the reaction too: a quick frame shudder in the punch's direction as it lands covers small alignment slips and makes the hit feel heavier, as if the whole world gets knocked sideways [S1]. Actors also remain aware of the camera at all times and alter their technique so the moment reads [S9].

## Timing: one clean beat

The ideal punch is a single readable action-reaction unit: one attack event, one defense or reaction, then a hold or recovery — "**one clean beat**, no flurry" [S5]. The handbooks' directorial-language crosswalk makes the timing logic concrete:

| Directorial intent | Punch-realism mechanism | Timing logic |
|---|---|---|
| "A fast right cross that nearly misses" | near-contact, readable line, fist trajectory, minimum distance, camera projection | strike reads fast but visibly clears |
| "He absorbs the hit, then decides to fall" | impulse proxy, torso recoil, decision beat, fall trajectory | involuntary recoil separated from chosen surrender |
| "Make it brutal but not faster" | larger momentum exchange, reaction amplitude, sound and camera impulse | duration locked; force added elsewhere, not by speeding up |
| "One clean beat, no flurry" | one attack event, one defense/reaction, hold or recovery | extra strikes and limb motion suppressed |

Two-character timing and screen direction are designed elements in their own right [S3], and fight beats should be built for readable contact and cause-effect storytelling [S7]. Timing also carries character information: fighters who "know each other" show reduced reaction latency, shared rhythm, and gaze prediction, so a delayed fall reads as a decision rather than a reflex [S5].

One thing the books never supply is a number: no frame counts or millisecond windows for the contact-to-response gap. The guidance stays qualitative — "one clean beat," a "decision beat," duration "locked" — so the timing is a craftsmanship judgment to be tuned on set, not a fixed measurement.
